title: Cryptanalysis
body:
Breaking ciphers rather than building them. The half of the course that makes the other half
honest: you cannot argue a cipher is strong without knowing what an attack looks like, and every
design decision in [[AES]] and [[RSA]] exists because some earlier scheme fell to one of these.

The founding observation, and the reason the whole classical block collapses: **natural language
is not uniform, and any cipher that preserves its statistics leaks the plaintext.** Cryptanalysis
is applied statistics before it is anything else, so it is [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) pointed at an
adversary.

## Frequency analysis

English letter frequencies are stable over any text long enough to matter:

```
E  12.7%     T  9.1%     A  8.2%     O  7.5%     I  7.0%
...
Z  0.07%     Q  0.10%    X  0.15%
```

A monoalphabetic cipher (shift, affine, general substitution) applies one fixed permutation to the
alphabet, so it **permutes the frequency table without changing it**. Count the ciphertext letters,
sort, and the most common symbol is almost certainly `E`. Digrams (`TH`, `HE`, `IN`) and trigrams
(`THE`, `AND`) pin down the rest.

This is why $26!$ keys buys nothing. The key space is astronomically large and the attack does not
search it: it *reads the key off the ciphertext*, one letter at a time. **Key space is a necessary
condition for security and never a sufficient one**, which is the single most transferable fact in
the course.

## Index of coincidence

The tool for the polyalphabetic case, where the frequency table has been flattened. $IC$ is the
probability that two characters drawn at random from the text are the same:

$$IC = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{25} n_i(n_i - 1)}{n(n-1)}$$

| Text | $IC$ |
|---|--:|
| English plaintext | $\approx 0.067$ |
| Monoalphabetic ciphertext | $\approx 0.067$ (unchanged) |
| Random / uniform | $\approx 0.038$ |
| Vigenère, long key | between the two, falling as the key lengthens |

Two uses, and they are the whole technique:

1. **Classify the cipher.** $IC \approx 0.067$ means monoalphabetic (or a
   [[Transposition Cipher]], which also preserves frequencies). $IC$ near 0.038 means
   polyalphabetic or better.
2. **Recover the key length.** Split the ciphertext into $m$ columns for $m = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ and
   compute the $IC$ of each column. When $m$ is the true Vigenère key length, every column is a
   single Caesar shift, so each column's $IC$ jumps back to 0.067. Wrong $m$ leaves the columns
   mixed and the $IC$ low.

Once $m$ is known, the polyalphabetic cipher is $m$ independent monoalphabetic ones and step 1
finishes it. **Kasiski examination** gets $m$ a different way: repeated ciphertext substrings are
usually the same plaintext encrypted at the same key offset, so the distances between repeats are
multiples of $m$, and $\gcd$ of those distances is the candidate. That is the
[[Euclidean Algorithm]] used as an attack.

## The attack models

What the adversary is assumed to have. Security claims are meaningless without one, and later
blocks quantify security *against a named model*.

| Model | The attacker has |
|---|---|
| Ciphertext-only | intercepted ciphertext, nothing else |
| Known-plaintext | some plaintext/ciphertext pairs |
| Chosen-plaintext | can encrypt plaintexts of their choosing |
| Chosen-ciphertext | can decrypt ciphertexts of their choosing (except the target) |

They climb in strength, and a cipher that survives chosen-ciphertext attack survives the others.
Modern schemes are expected to hold at the top of the ladder even though real adversaries usually
sit at the bottom, because the assumption costs nothing and the mistake is unrecoverable.

Two more facts the block sets up:

- **Brute force is the baseline attack every cipher must beat.** A cipher with an $n$-bit key is
  broken in $2^n$ work by definition, and "secure" means "no attack does better". DES's 56-bit key
  fell to exactly this, which is why [[AES]] starts at 128 bits. See [[Time Complexity]] for why
  $2^{128}$ is not a large number in the way $2^{56}$ was.
- **Hard is not the same as NP-hard.** [[NP-Complete]] (COMP 2613) is a *worst-case* notion: an
  NP-hard problem has hard instances, and may still be easy on almost all of them. Cryptography
  needs the opposite guarantee, that a *randomly chosen* instance is hard, which is why
  [[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] and factoring are the assumptions of choice even though neither is
  known to be NP-complete.
